title: Netanyahu Places NYC Mayor Mamdani on Tel Aviv Billboard Alongside Iran's Ayatollah and Hezbollah Chief
excerpt: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's re-election campaign features Indian-American Mayor Zohran Mamdani alongside Iran's Supreme Leader and Hezbollah's chief with the message: 'They want Netanyahu to lose.'
body:
• Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's re-election campaign has placed a massive billboard on Tel Aviv's Ayalon highway showing NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani alongside Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem, and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
  • The billboard reads "They want Netanyahu to lose. Don't let them win" — framing foreign critics as campaign assets in Israel's upcoming election.
  • Mamdani, NYC's first Indian-American and first Muslim mayor, has repeatedly called Netanyahu a "war criminal" and explored whether the city could enforce an ICC arrest warrant.
  • The move elevates an American municipal leader to the same category as heads of state and militant organizations in Israeli domestic politics.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's re-election campaign has placed New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani — the city's first Indian-American and first Muslim mayor — on a massive billboard in central Tel Aviv alongside some of Israel's most prominent adversaries.

The billboard, erected on the Ayalon highway, one of Tel Aviv's busiest thoroughfares, shows Mamdani's image alongside Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem, and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. The caption reads: "They want Netanyahu to lose. Don't let them win."

A Familiar Playbook

The billboard is not the first time Netanyahu's Likud party has invoked Mamdani during its re-election campaign. The prime minister previously used the NYC mayor's vocal opposition — including Mamdani's characterization of Netanyahu as "a war criminal" — as a virtual endorsement in a campaign advertisement capped with the same message.

The tactic follows a well-established pattern in Israeli politics, where leaders have long used foreign criticism to rally domestic support. But placing an American city mayor alongside a designated terrorist organization's leader and the supreme leader of a nation Israel considers an existential threat marks an unusual escalation.

The Mamdani-Netanyahu Clash

The tension between the two leaders has been building for months. In July, Mamdani posted a video calling Netanyahu "the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people" and directed the city's legal department to investigate whether the NYPD could enforce the International Criminal Court's arrest warrant against the Israeli prime minister if he entered New York for the United Nations General Assembly in September.

Mamdani later acknowledged that New York City does not have the independent legal authority to arrest a visiting foreign leader on international charges. President Donald Trump separately declared that Netanyahu would not be arrested "in any way, shape, or form" while in the United States.

"I will not be welcoming Benjamin Netanyahu or any other war criminals when they come to this city, and I do believe that our federal government should join the International Criminal Court."

— Zohran Mamdani, Mayor of New York City

An Indian-American on the Global Stage

Mamdani's appearance on an Israeli campaign billboard underscores the remarkable global profile achieved by the 34-year-old mayor, who was born in Kampala, Uganda, to parents of Indian descent — his father Mahmood Mamdani is a renowned Columbia University professor, and his mother is acclaimed Indian filmmaker Mira Nair, known for "Mississippi Masala" and "Monsoon Wedding."

The family was part of Uganda's Indian diaspora community. Mamdani moved to New York City at age seven, grew up in Queens, and attended the Bronx High School of Science before graduating from Bowdoin College. He served as a New York State Assemblymember before his upset victory in the 2025 mayoral race, defeating former Governor Andrew Cuomo in the Democratic primary.

His election made him not only the first Indian-American and first Muslim mayor of New York City but also one of the most prominent Indian-origin elected officials in the United States. His stance on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict has drawn both fierce criticism from Jewish organizations and strong support from progressive voters and the city's large Muslim community.

Divided Reactions

Mamdani's rhetoric on Israel has sparked reactions well beyond politics. NBA star Kyle Kuzma publicly criticized the mayor as "a mayor playing president," while Dallas Mavericks guard Kyrie Irving and San Antonio Spurs star Victor Wembanyama were seen liking Mamdani's Instagram post calling for Netanyahu's arrest.

Mamdani, who is reportedly on vacation in upstate New York, has yet to comment on Netanyahu's use of his image in the campaign billboard. The Israeli election is expected in the coming months, with Netanyahu facing pressure from multiple directions, including the ongoing war in Gaza and domestic political challenges.
